title: Deformation Mechanisms of a TiHfZrNbTa High Entropy Superelastic Alloy by In Situ Synchrotron Based DCT and 3DXRD Techniques

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: In 2015, Firstov et al. [ 1 ] introduced a new class of alloys that combines High Entropy with Shape Memory effect (HESMA). These alloys benefit from the synergistic advantages of both effects and offer improved performance in terms of strength, thermal stability and reversible deformation [ 2 ].

The high entropy effect has thus clearly increased the thermal stability compared to the binary alloys. This can be due to mechanical properties modification and/or the martensitic transformation crystallography, leading to an increase of the critical stress for martensitic transformation. It will therefore help to develop micromechanical models for the design of new HESMAs by predicting single crystal elastic constants, critical resolved shear stresses and following the martensitic transformation during thermomechanical loading.

Diffraction Contrast Tomography (DCT) [ 20 ] and 3-Dimensional X-ray Diffraction (3DXRD) [ 21 ] have been developed to obtain 3D information at grain scale. DCT allows a 3D mapping of grains providing shape, orientation and spatial position of all individual grains within a sample. Using the 3DXRD technique, the average elastic strain tensor can be determined for each grain and the stress tensor can thus be calculated using elastic constants of the single crystal. Moreover, the 3DXRD technique gives access to the center of mass location and orientation of each individual grain, which allow a grain tracking during a tensile test given a limited deviation upon these two parameters between two loading steps. These techniques have been successfully applied to study intrinsic mechanisms of plasticity at the grain scale [ 22 ,  23 ] or fatigue crack [ 24 ]. Moreover, martensitic transformation at grain scale was also successfully characterized for different SMAs such as CuAlBe [ 25 ], CuAlNi [ 26 ,  27 ], NiTi [ 28 ,  29 – 30 ], and more recently for a metastable high entropy alloy [ 31 ].

The combined use of DCT and 3DXRD is the most polyvalent and complete method to fully characterize in 3D the martensitic transformation of SMAs. It is a real improvement compared to classical 2D in-situ characterization based on 2D-EBSD measurements which only detect in-plane phase transformation [ 32 ,  33 ].

On the numerical side, El Hachi et al. [ 25 ] successfully developed a 3D digital twin of a CuAlBe SMA based on a combined synchrotron investigation, which was used to reconstruct the full volume of a polycrystal. Combined with a micromechanical model, finite-element simulations yielded relatable results regarding macroscopic and grain-level responses, and further highlighted the neighboring effect on the initiation of martensite formation.

The paper is structured as follows: the next section presents “ Materials and Methods ” used in terms of material preparation, 3D imaging techniques and test conditions. “ Results ” section is then presented, scaling down from the macroscopic to the grain scale. The final section “ Discussion ”, discusses both results and effects of crystallographic orientation.

sections.heading: Material and Sample Preparation
paragraphs: The HESMA is superelastic at ambient temperature. To characterize its grain-resolved mechanical behavior, in-situ tests were done using synchrotron radiation. Uniaxial tensile tests were performed stepwise with the force-controlled Nanox tensile device developed by Gueninchault et al. [ 34 ] and illustrated in Fig.  1 a. The tensile specimen was cut using Electrical Discharge Machining (EDM) to fit constraints of the Nanox tensile machine; the thickness was set to 0.18 mm and the width to 0.3 mm in order to limit the number of diffracting grains in the scanned volume. The macroscopic load was measured using a load cell. Macroscopic strain was measured using particle tracking, which is based on a surface feature displacement.

The results presented are from the MA5410 experimental campaign conducted on ID11 beamline at ESRF in September 2022. For comprehensive details on the methodology and experimental setup, refer to the open-access dataset published by ESRF [ 35 ].

sections.heading: DCT and 3DXRD Preparation
paragraphs: The main goal of the study was to identify material parameters depicting the elastic behavior and the onset of the martensitic transformation. A dedicated methodology was deployed to achieve the final task of having a micromechanical response able to compute the critical resolved stress of the studied material. The methodology was divided into several successive steps: (i) Evolution of austenitic grain indexations during loading; (ii) Measurements of the grain elastic strain tensor based on lattice distortion; (iii) Definition of a micromechanical model of the material; (iv) Identification of single-crystal elastic constants based on grain strains in the elastic domain; (v) Computations of macroscopic responses in the inelastic domain; (vi) Computation of the critical resolved shear stress in potential privileged crystallographic orientations for the martensitic transformation. Note that the section “ Results ”, containing tasks (i) and (ii), is dedicated to the experimental part while the “ Discussions ” section, containing tasks (iii-vi), is devoted to the numerical part. sections.heading: Grain Indexation
paragraphs: Figure  3  illustrates the initial microstructure of the specimen prior to the in-situ test colored by grain orientation. In Fig.  3 a, Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM) micrograph reveals a microstructure composed of equiaxed grains, with an average grain size on the order of several tens of micrometers. The image has been captured by a Zeiss Supra 40 SEM, using secondary electrons with a voltage of 20 kV. The microstructure of the initial state was further reconstructed using DCT, as shown in Fig.  3 b.

At the initial state, a total of 662 grains were indexed by DCT, and 816 grains by 3DXRD. The difference between these two techniques is explained by the fact that for DCT, only grains totally included in the scanned volume were kept for the following analysis while incomplete grains located at upper and lower boundaries were not considered (see Fig.  3 b). This consideration was not applied to the 3DXRD results, as this technique only provides information about the position of the center of mass, rather than the exact shape of the grains.

Figure  4  shows the evolution of the number of indexed grains with respect to the loading step. The percentage of indexed grains has been calculated using the initial number of indexed grains for both techniques.

Both techniques are in good agreement as they show the same tendency to decrease the percentage of indexed grains above a stress of 492 MPa. The two observed regions (elastic and inelastic) of the tensile curve (Fig.  4 ) can then be correlated with the percentage of indexed grains. The percentage does not decrease during the elastic part and then decreases sharply during the inelastic part. During the unloading part, some of the grains that were no longer indexed are recovered.

Discussion
paragraphs: This section discusses stress analysis at macroscopic and grain scales. First, elastic constants of the material were determined from 3DXRD measurements, which enabled the calculation of each grain stress tensor at each loading step. The results are discussed in terms of the crystallographic orientation in the second part.

sections.heading: Numerical Results

paragraphs: Then, for the inelastic part both binary and quaternary parameters overestimate experimental stresses while accurately capturing stiffness changes. However, values in this work better match data-points.

On the one hand, the macroscopic stress is experimentally captured from the whole probe volume (austenite and martensite), whereas, on the other hand, stress calculations took only into account the austenite elastic strain contribution for each grain captured by 3DXRD. The decrease in macroscopic stress is likely due to the inelastic phenomena of partially transformed grains. Indeed, only the austenite phase has been indexed and the martensite formation could modify locally the austenite intragranular strain since shear stress components start to develop as observed by El Hachi et al. for a CuAlBe superelastic alloy [ 25 ]. In addition, as grains transform, their volumes decrease and become too low to be detected by diffraction techniques: they are no longer indexed, and, consequently, do not contribute to the global stress calculation. For these reasons, the global stress decreases due to a contribution of non-indexed grains and a possible contribution of the martensite phase which is not taken into account. This shift between austenite mean stress and applied macroscopic stress was also previously observed in a CuAlBe SMA [ 25 ]. As the martensitic transformation is depending on the crystallographic orientation, the last section explores the behavior of similarly oriented grains.
